elements.text: Aerodynamic stall and subsequent uncommanded roll during one-engine-inoperative takeoff flight test
Gulfstream's failure to properly develop and validate takeoff speeds for flight tests
Gulfstream's failure to recognize and correct the takeoff safety speed (V2) error during previous G650 flight tests
G650 flight test team's persistent and increasingly aggressive attempts to achieve erroneously low V2 speeds
Gulfstream's inadequate investigation of previous G650 uncommanded roll events
Company's overestimation of stall angle of attack while the airplane was in ground effect
Gulfstream's failure to effectively manage the G650 flight test program
Pursuing an aggressive program schedule without ensuring defined roles and responsibilities
Insufficient technical planning and oversight of engineering processes
Failure to fully identify potential hazards
Failure to implement and ensure functioning of appropriate risk controls
Test team's focus on achieving takeoff safety speeds and lack of guidance on pitch angle targets contributed to exceeding limits
Stall on the right outboard wing produced a right rolling moment that the flight crew was not able to control
Airplane stalled at an angle of attack below the predicted in-ground-effect stall AOA and stick shaker activation threshold
Gulfstream's decision to use an inappropriate takeoff speed development method from a previous program
Gulfstream's failure to perform rigorous root cause analysis of difficulties in achieving G650 takeoff safety speeds
Gulfstream had sufficient information from previous tests to determine target V2 speeds could not be achieved with certifiable technique
Deficiencies in Gulfstream's technical planning and oversight contributed to incorrect speeds used on the day of the accident
Failure to clearly define roles and responsibilities for on-site test team members led to inadequate monitoring of safety parameters
Gulfstream's focus on meeting the certification date caused schedule-related pressure not counterbalanced by robust organizational processes
Gulfstream's flight test safety program was deficient due to insufficient risk controls and lacking safety assurance activities
Flight crew's response to the stall event was understandable given low altitude, time-critical nature, and ambiguous stall cues
Impact forces were survivable, but cabin environment became unsurvivable due to fuel, vapor, smoke, and fire
Manufacturers should consider potential for lower maximum lift coefficient in ground effect when estimating stall AOA
Effective flight test standard operating policies and procedures would help reduce inherent risks
Flight test safety management system guidance tailored to manufacturers would help promote effective safety programs
External safety audits would help monitor implementation of safety management principles
Knowledge of lessons learned from Gulfstream's implementation would enhance flight test safety
Advance coordination between flight test operators and airport operations/firefighting personnel could reduce response time
